FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS

PART III: FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS [Article 12-35]

Fundamental rights are a set of legally enforceable rights.

Salient Features of Fundamental Rights

Fundamental Rights —

  • are not absolute. (but have limits)
  • are not 'Sacrosanct' or Permanent.
  • can be curtailed during emergency. (but Article 20 and 21 can never be suspended)
  • are justiciable in nature.

Basic Pointers

  • They are borrowed from the Constitution of USA. (Bill of Rights).
  • They are contained in Part III of the Constitution → Article (12-35)
  • They are termed as "Conscience of Constitution"
  • They seek to implement political democracy.
  • They are referred to as the "Magna Carta of India"
  • Originally there were 7 fundamental rights, currently there are 6 Fundamental Rights (Right to property was removed from Part III in 1978 by 44th CA, It is now a legal right under Article 300-A, part XII.)

Six Fundamental Rights given in the constitution are:

  • Right to Equality: Article 14-18
  • Right to Freedom: Article 19-22
  • Right against Exploitation: Article 23-24
  • Right to Freedom of Religion: Article 25-28
  • Cultural and Educational Rights: Article 29-30
  • Right to Constitutional Remedies: Article 32

Fundamental Rights in detail:

Article 12: Definition of State

  • It defines the term "State" which includes the Government, Union executive, the Parliament of India, the Legislature of each of the sates, and all local or other authorities within the territory of India.

Article 13: Laws Inconsistent with or in Derogation of the Fundamental Rights

  • Any law made before the commencement of constitution shall be declared null and void by judiciary if it violates Fundamental Rights.
  • Law includes any ordinance, order, by-law, rule, regulation, notification, in the territory of India.
  • This article shall not apply to any amendment made under Article 368.

Article 14-18: Right to Equality

Article 14: Equality before Law and Equal Protection of laws

  • Exception: President, MLAs/MPs, governor, foreigner dignitaries cannot be arrested in civil/criminal matters.
  • A. V. Dicey considered equality before the law to be a fundamental principle of Rule of Law.
Equality Before LawEqual Protection of Law
This is a negative concept taken from the UK.This is a positive concept taken from USA.
States that everyone should be treated equally in the eyes of the law.Like should be treated alike under the law.

Article 15: Prohibition of Discrimination on Grounds of Religion, Race, Caste, Sex or Place of Birth

  • 15(1) The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth.
  • 15(2) No citizen shall, on these grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to—
  • (a) Access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment; or
  • (b) The use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds.
  • 15(3) the State can make special provisions for women and children, e.g. few Metro seats are reserved for women.
  • 15(4) the State can make special provision for the advancement of Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes.

Article 16: Equality of Opportunity in Matters of Public Employment

  • (1) Equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the state.
  • (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the state.
  • (3) State can set rule that gives preference to people who are residents of the area when it comes to local employment or appointments.
  • (4) State can make rules to reserve jobs or positions for "backward classes" who are underrepresented in the state services.

Cases/Commission subjective to article 16(4):

  • Kalelkar Commission (1953)

→ 1st Backward Class commission (Chairman: Kaka Kalelkar)

  • Mandal Commission (1979)

→ 2nd Backward Class commission (Chairman: B P Mandal)

→ Recommended 27% reservation to OBCs

→ Implemented by Prime Minister V.P. Singh in 1990.

  • Indra Sawhney Case (1992) - also known as Mandal case.

→ Public Interest Litigation by advocate Indira Sawhney.

→ The Supreme Court upheld the 27% reservation for OBCs in government job, but also set a 50% cap on total reservations.

→ Creamy-layer is to be identified in OBC are not entitled to reservation.

Public Interest Litigation (PIL) is taken from USA's constitution.

FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS (Continued)

Article 17: Abolition of Untouchability

  • The state and any private individual are prohibited from practicing untouchability.
  • The term 'Untouchability' has nowhere been defined in the constitution.

Article 18: Abolition of Titles

  • No title, other than being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State.
  • No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign state.
  • No person, holding any office of profit shall receive "Title" from any foreign state without the consent of the President.
  • Eg: Maharaja, Rai Bahadur, etc.

Article 19-22: Right to Freedom

Article 19: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.

TRICK - SAAMRO

  • (1) All citizens shall have the right—
  • S → (a) to freedom of speech and expression — "Hallmark of Democracy"
  • A → (b) to assemble peacefully and without arms;
  • A → (c) to form associations or unions or cooperative societies;
  • M → (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India
  • R → (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India;
  • O → (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business.
  • (2) Reasonable restriction can be imposed in interest of Public order, decency, morality, sovereignty, integrity, defamation, contempt of court etc.

Hidden Rights under Article 19:

  • Right to Internet (Anuradha Bhasin vs Union of India case, 2020)
  • Right to Information (Raj Narayan vs State of UP, 1975)
  • 97th Amendment added Right to form Cooperative societies under Article 19(1)(c)
  • Article 19(f), Right to Property, has been omitted by 44th CA, 1978.

Article 20: Protection in respect of conviction for Offences

  • (1) No ex-post-facto law: No person shall be subject to a penalty greater than that prescribed by law in force when the crime was committed.
  • (2) No double jeopardy: A person must not be punished twice for the same offence.
  • (3) No self-incrimination: A person cannot be compelled to provide information or testify against oneself. But have to submit blood specimen or thumb impressions, if asked.

Article 21: Protection of Life and Personal Liberty

  • No person shall be deprived of his life except according to the procedure established by law. (Borrowed from the Japanese constitution)
  • The foremost right among right to freedom is Right to life and Personal Liberty.

Article 20 and 21 can never be suspended.

Landmark Cases & Interpretations

A. K. Gopalan Case: 1950

  • The Supreme Court of India took a narrow view of Article 21 and ruled that it does not guarantees "Due process of law."

Maneka Gandhi Case: 1967

  • The Supreme Court overturned the Gopalan case ruling.
  • Took a wide stance on Article 21 and introduced the "Due Process of Law."
  • It expanded the interpretation of Article 21 and made Right to Travel abroad - a Fundamental Right to personal liberty.
  • Included some rights under Article 21 namely Right to Health, Shelter, Speedy trial, Information, Sleep, Electricity, Privacy

KS Puttaswamy case affirmed that the Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of right to life and personal liberty.

'Due Process of Law': ensures fair and just legal proceedings. It is not mentioned in Constitution and is an American concept.

Article 21(A): Right to Education

  • Added by 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002
  • It guarantees the right to free and compulsory education for children between the ages of 6 and 14.

Article 22: Protection against Arrest & Detention in certain cases

  • A person being arrested under ordinary law has:
  • Right to be informed.
  • Right to be defended by a legal practitioner.
  • Right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hrs.
  • Right to be released after 24 hours unless the magistrate authorises for their detention.

Punitive Detention: Occurs after a crime has been committed.

Preventive detention: To prevent a possible future offence. This detention cannot exceed 3 months, unless an Advisory Board of High Court judges approves an extension.

Article 23-24: Right against Exploitation

Article 23: Prohibition of trafficking in Human Beings and Forced Labour (Beggar)

  • Exception: State can force people to do compulsory services, for e.g. during War.

Article 24: Prohibition of Employment of Children in Hazardous Places

  • No child below the age of 14 years shall be employed in Factories, Mines or any other hazardous occupations.
  • They can however work at safe places during non-school hours.

Article 25-28: Right to freedom of Religion

Article 25: Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice and Propagation of Religion

Article 26: Freedom to Manage Religious Affairs

  • Every religious institution or section shall have the right to:
  • (a) Establish and maintain religious institutions.
  • (b) Manage their own religious affairs.
  • (c) Own and acquire movable and immovable property.
  • (d) Administer property in accordance with law.
  • Article 26 also guarantees collective freedom of religion.

FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS (Continued)

Article 27: Freedom as to Payment of Taxes for Promotion of Any Particular Religion

  • This provision prohibits only the levy of taxes and not fee.

Article 28: Freedom from attending Religious Instruction

  • No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly funded by the State.

Article 29-30: Cultural and Educational Rights

Article 29: Protection of Interest of Minorities

  • Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script, or culture has the right to conserve it.

Article 30: Rights of Minorities to establish and administer educational Institutions

  • The state cannot discriminate based on religion or language while providing aid.

Article 29 is not solely specific to minorities whereas Article 30 is specifically for minorities. Term 'Minority' is nowhere defined in constitution.

Article 32-35: Right to Constitutional Remedies

Article 32: Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this part

  1. 1. Right to approach the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
  2. 2. Supreme Court's powers: The Supreme Court can issue orders, directions, or writs to enforce fundamental rights. These writs include Habeas corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-warranto.

Writ Jurisdiction SC vs HC:

Supreme Court (Article 32)High Court (Article 226)
The SC cannot refuse to issue writ.The HC can refuse to issue writ.
It can only issue writs when there is violation of Fundamental Rights only.It can issue writs when there is violation of Fundamental Rights + Legal Rights (hence, writ jurisdiction of HC is wider).
Jurisdiction: Throughout the territory of India.Jurisdiction: Throughout the state
  • Parliament can authorise any other court other than SC & HC to issue writs.

Five writs issued by the Supreme Court (and High Courts) under Article 32 and Article 226 of the Indian Constitution are:

Habeas Corpus - "to have the body of"

  • It ensures individual liberty against unlawful detention.
  • ADM Jabalpur case is also known as Habeas Corpus case, it is related to 'Personal Liberty'.

Mandamus - "We command"

  • Orders a public official or authority to perform a duty they failed to do.
  • It cannot be issued against: a private individual, President, Governor, or when the duty is not mandatory.

Prohibition - "To forbid"

  • Issued by a superior court to a lower court to prevent the latter from exceeding its jurisdiction.

Certiorari - "To be certified"

  • Issued by a higher court to transfer a case pending in the lower court to itself or nullifies the lower court's order if it acted beyond jurisdiction.

Quo Warranto - "By what authority"

  • Challenges a person's right to hold a public office.

Dr. B. R. Ambedkar mentioned Article 32 as "Heart and Soul" of Indian Constitution.

Article 33

  • It empowers the parliament to restrict the Fundamental Rights for the members of Armed Forces, Police and Intelligence Agencies to ensure proper discipline and duty. (50th amendment, 1984)

Article 34

  • It provides for the restrictions on Fundamental Rights while Martial Law is enforced in an area.

Martial Law borrowed from: UK

Article 35

  • It vests exclusive powers in parliament to make laws relating to enforcement of certain fundamental rights.

Rights that are available only to the citizen of India and not to Foreigners - Article 15, 16, 19, 29, 30
